# Earthquakes in Chile 

CRU’s thoughts and condolences go out to our colleagues and people of Chile affected by the recent earthquake and tremors. Chile is world’s largest copper producer and accounts for around 35% of global mine output.  In 2009, Chilean copper mine production was 5.36Mt of which 3.25Mt was copper-inconcentrates and 2.11Mt EW cathode. 

On Monday 1<sup>st</sup> March, the copper price hit a 5-week peak of $7,600/t in early trading on the LME due to concerns over supply following the 8.8 magnitude earthquake that shook Chile on Saturday 27<sup>th</sup> February. In the following days, several aftershocks of magnitudes up to 6.1 have been shaking the regions from Santiago to the south.  In addition, on the evening of Thursday 4<sup>th</sup> March a 6.3 earthquake close to Calama shook the northern regions.  Infrastructure that was not damaged by the earthquakes is still at risk. Foremost, power cuts continue throughout the country but miners say that they are not affected. 

The earthquake had minor impacts on Chilean copper production.  Only a few mines and smelters suffered minor damage and no victims have been reported at these operations.  Logistics have been affected (road, rail and ports) and power disruptions interrupted production.  In more detail: 





- No major damage to mining or smelting operations.  Most of the major copper operations are located in the northern regions. 

- Power cuts halted production and there is still the possibility of further disruptions during the next few weeks. 



- Other infrastructure damage include ports and roads.

## **Mines and smelters: not major damages** 

Overall, copper mines and smelters were not significantly affected by the earthquake, although some of them had minor rock slides and damage. 

Operations in the regions north of Santiago – where most of the copper is produced – were unaffected. However, on the evening of Thursday 4<sup>th</sup> March a 6.3 earthquake close to Calama shook the northern regions. Codelco said that no damage was registered at their Codelco Norte Division. At the time of writing, there were few indications of whether there has been any loss of production at mines or smelters. 

Disruptions are a possibility inmediately after any aftershock.  BHP Billiton, Barrick Gold, Xstrata and Teck all stated that their operations have not suffered any damage after the original earthquake.  The major risk for the next week or so continues to be a shortage of diesel, which would halt power generation at mines that rely on diesel generators and mining operations (trucks in particular ).  Key copper ports of Antofagasta and Mejillones are said to be operating normally. 

Some operations in the regions south of Santiago suffered minor damages after the original earthquake. Copper operations have not suffered any major damage, but those located near Santiag

o (El Teniente, Andina, El Soldado, Los Bronces and Mantoverde mines; and Chagres and Ventanas smelter) halted production mainly because of the power cut on Saturday. It was reported, however, that on Sunday (28th ) afternoon some mines resumed operations. Anglo American said that production losses were less than 1,500t of contained copper. For instance, CAP (main steel producer) will stop its operations for at least three months and Anglo American informed that its grinding media plant located close to Concepcion was seriously damaged. ## **Shortages of energy to remain a risk in the aftermath** The big question has been about the state of the country’s power facilities, oil refineries and general energy availability. Chile has four power grids dominated by SING ( _Sistema Interconectado del Norte Grande_ ) and SIC ( _Sistema Interconectado Central_ ). SING supplies power to all the mines in the northern regions, while SIC supplies power to the central and southern regions, where the main earthquake took place. The power problems at the SIC affected Los Pelambres, Mantoverde, Andina, El Soldado and El Teniente mines; as well as Chagres smelter. No problemas were reported in the SING. © 2010 CRU International Ltd **confidential** Page 2 of 6 **March 2010** www.crumonitor.com Problems at the nation’s oil refineries could conceivably disrupt supplies to generators and to the country. There has been minor damage to power generation facilities but potential problems with transmission and distribution of electricity may affect some operations. It was reported that state-owned oil company ENAP suspended operations at Chile’s two oil refineries Bнo Bнo (damage to inf

rastructure) and Aconcagua (power shortages). Bio-Bio is located south of Santiago and Aconcagua is located north-west of Santiago. ENAP assured consumers that it has a twelve-day supply of fuels and has already started to import diesel and gasoline to meet demand. According to the company, Aconcagua could resume operations next week while Bio-Bio’s restart date is still unknown given the scale of the damage. If the 12-day stocks run out, there is a possibility that the company will be challenged to meet the country’s demands. ## **Other infrastructure** CRU understands that roads and ports are in good condition in the northern regions following the original earthquake, but at the time of writing there is limited information of the situation after the Thursday (4th March) quake. In the southern regions, close to the epicentre of the original earthquake, activities in the ports were suspended, but started to partially resume operations during the week. The port of San Antonio was closed and as of Wednesday only two of the eight piers were operating, while the others are expected to resume operation in the following weeks. Roads that connect Santiago with the south of the country have been affected. # Copper production - In Chile, copper production increased by 5% y-o-y in December 2009 according to Cochilco. This is the fifth increase after thirteen consecutive months of declines. The year ended up with a 1% increase. In 2009, Codelco produced 235,6000t more mainly because of Codelco Norte (119,400t more y-o-y) as more concentrates were processed (from both own operations and third parties) and the ramp up of Gaby (80,300t more y-o-y). This was offset by Escondida as they produced 150,300t less (-12% y-o-y) as a result of the failure –and then repair- of its SAG mill at the Laguna Seca concentrator. Copper production at Collahuasi increased by 71,600t, a 15% rise y-o-y, due to the completion debottlenecking project. Spence showed a 12,600t decline in respect to November 2008 as the operation’s unionised workers were on strike for most of the month. - In Peru, copper production decreased by 5% y-o-y in January 2010.
